y4-ht2-je-peux.summary: Ten action verbs, « Je peux … », « Je ne peux pas … », « Tu peux … ? » and longer sentences with et / mais. Ends with Guess Who! and Mon bilan.

assessPlan.s5: Explains the pattern (ne … pas around peux; the verb after peux stays in the infinitive) and applies it to new verbs and to questions such as « Tu peux … ? ».

y3-ht1.summary: Greetings, feelings, name, numbers 1 to 10 and age (j'ai … ans). Lesson 1 Bienvenue au Monde Francophone (not assessed). Useful words: merci, oui, non. Extension: à plus tard, bonsoir, très bien / très mal; 11 to 20 as a challenge only.
y3-ht1.phonicsNote: One sound this half-term. About 3 sound words and 1 to 2 traps per lesson; retrieval only covers what has been taught so far. Lesson 5: nous, tout, toujours + trap “bon”. Silent final letters noticed informally (nous, trois); in six and dix the final x IS pronounced (/s/). Transcription: choice of 2.

y3-ht2.summary: 10 core colours, 5 per lesson, all from the song: rouge, jaune, bleu, vert, gris (Lesson 1) and orange, noir, blanc, violet, rose (Lesson 2). Taught as chunks, no agreement. Extension: marron. Numbers are not core (taught in HT1): quick recap only. Builds to « Quelle est ta couleur préférée ? », « Ma couleur préférée, c'est le … Et toi ? ». Uses “Les couleurs et les nombres” lessons 1 to 3 and the songs “Les couleurs” and “Quelle est ta couleur préférée ?”.
y3-ht2.phonicsNote: About 3 sound words and 1 to 2 traps per lesson. Suggested: L1 moi, toi, trois (trap: tout) · L2 noir, voilà, poisson (trap: bonjour) · L3 roi, boîte, froid · L4 pourquoi, voir, soir (trap: nous) · L5 étoile, oiseau, mois · L6 recap · L7 Christmas lesson, no phonics. Transcription: choice of 2.
y3-ht2.grammar: Chunks only. Colour after the noun comes in HT3.
y3-ht2.culture: Noël: le réveillon, la bûche de Noël, les marchés de Noël, le calendrier de l'Avent.

y3-ht3.summary: Core: chat, chien, cheval, canard, poisson, ours, souris (chosen for Ours brun and known sounds). Je suis + un/une + animal + colour. Extension: cochon, vache, mouton (“Les animaux” slides can support).

y4-ht2.summary: Our own unit, 6 lessons, with Marie and Pierre. Verbs (infinitives): danser, chanter, sauter, cuisiner, faire du vélo, jouer au foot, patiner, dessiner, nager, parler français; extension (all -er): jouer d'un instrument, jouer de la guitare, jouer au hockey, grimper, skier. Most end in -er (faire ends in -re). Je peux + infinitive; je ne peux pas; et / mais. « Tu peux … ? » with the Guess Who board. Negation (ne … pas) isolated and assessed. Marie and Pierre show what they can and can't do.

y4-ht3.summary: Intermediate unit (replaces “La date”). 8 pets: un chien, un chat, un lapin, un hamster, un poisson rouge, un oiseau, une souris, une tortue. J'ai … et …; qui s'appelle … (chunk); je n'ai pas de / d' … (chunk, not assessed); mais. Extra j'ai practice; links to HT6 third person. “La date” (months, 21 to 31) is left to Years 5 to 6; the days of the week come with La Chenille (HT4).
y4-ht3.soundHint: as in chat, souris, pas, chez
y4-ht3.soundSays: the last consonant is usually silent
y4-ht3.phonicsNote: Silent final consonants revisited and formalised: chat, souris, pas, chez. “CaReFuL” exceptions c, r, f, l are often said (e.g. hamster, neuf). Trapdoor game: “Is the last letter silent?” Transcription: free, building to checkpoint 3.
y4-ht3.grammar: J'ai + noun; qui s'appelle and je n'ai pas de as chunks.
y4-ht3.culture: Geography & landmarks: the Eiffel Tower and a few French regions and cities.

page.intro: How the French scheme for Years 3 and 4 is built: what we want pupils to achieve, how every lesson works, the activities we use, and how learning builds over two years.
intent: French is fun and engaging, and built on evidence of what makes language learning stick, not only what makes it enjoyable.

Pupils grow the confidence to listen, speak and hold real conversations. The audience grows on purpose: a partner, a small group, the class, then parents or an assembly, older pupils, and finally a new teacher.
A planned cultural strand with several touchpoints each year, tied to units and the calendar, not left to chance.
A have-a-go culture, supported by quick checks every lesson, so pupils and teachers know where they stand long before any test.
page.pillars: Phonics, vocabulary and grammar are taught as three explicit, interwoven strands. Phonics and retrieval always come before new language.
lesson: Read known and new words with the sound of the half term aloud (decoding).
Hear it, write it: the same sounds the other way round (encoding).
Picture → say the French. Spaced and mixed so pupils know more and remember more.
New language one item at a time, big in the middle, then all together (Tous ensemble).
Guided practice: games, songs, paired talk and worked examples.
Independent work: write first, then draw. Assessment evidence is gathered here.
How did it go? What's next? « Au revoir ! » and « Où est Pierre ? ».
research: The National Curriculum for languages (Key Stage 2)
The statutory programme of study: listening, speaking, reading, writing and grammar. Every unit is assessed against its codes.
Teaching Schools Council: MFL Pedagogy Review (2016)
Phonics, vocabulary and grammar taught explicitly and practised often, which is why they are the three strands of every unit.
NCELP (National Centre for Excellence for Language Pedagogy)
Teaching sound, vocabulary and grammar systematically, and revisiting earlier language through spaced retrieval.
SEND Code of Practice (2015) and EEF guidance on SEN in mainstream schools
Behind the Inclusion work: high-quality teaching for every pupil, adapted so that all pupils can take part in the same lesson.
Cognitive load theory (routines and small steps so children are not overwhelmed), dual coding (the French word paired with its picture) and the SOLO taxonomy of Biggs and Collis, used for assessment.
Phonics, vocabulary and grammar as the three pillars of progress.
Daily review, new material in small steps, guided then independent practice.
Retrieval practice, spacing and interleaving to reduce cognitive load.
The phonics games used every day: Pause and Say, Phonic Bingo…
vocabulary: A small, useful core set (anchored to the words pupils will need later at GCSE). Every pupil is taught and assessed on it.
A few extra words each pupil chooses, kept in a 'mes mots' corner of the word mat. A deliberate way to keep every pupil, including boys and disadvantaged pupils, interested.
Words are revisited, connected and reused across units rather than taught as one-off topic lists.

phonics: Teacher shows a word; pause; everyone says it together.
Bingo boards of sound words; listen and cover.
Collect words that share the same sound.
Pupils hold word cards and find others with the same sound.
lesson: Point at a picture on the board and say a word. If it is the right word for the picture, the class repeats it; if it is the wrong word, they stay silent. Sometimes a child leads at the board.

Two real toys with their own personalities, who only speak French. Marie (a teddy) is shy, timid, calm and quiet. Her best friend Pierre (a toy duck) is loud, cheeky and outgoing. Hold one up and pupils speak or sing to match: quiet for Marie, loud for Pierre, especially during songs. Pupils talk to them and ask them questions in French. A child who is upset or feeling down can keep Marie or Pierre at their table. Pierre also hides for the game « Où est Pierre ? », which pupils love.
Ask yes/no questions to find a hidden character: on the board first, then in pairs.
Two pupils race to splat the picture of the word they hear.
Picture or word boards; the caller says the French and pupils cover it.
Learn the unit song, then fill in missing words in the lyrics.
One picture disappears; pupils say which one has gone.
Pupils make the cards, then say the French every time they turn one.
Roll for a picture (and a colour); say the full sentence.
Sort words or pictures into groups, then explain the choice.
Answer the question, say « Et toi ? » and throw the ball to someone new.
Ask friends a question and record the answers; look at the results together.
Find your partner's ships by saying grid words in French.
Short dialogues with puppets or in role (café, interview…).
Retrieval games to recall vocabulary quickly.
Find French clues around the room or playground.
assess: The end-of-unit written check (Lesson 6), done with nothing on display, in Class, Adapted and Inclusion versions. It gives the written evidence for the unit's reading, writing and grammar codes.
Speaking and listening codes are judged during planned activities: the survey, Guess Who!, songs, conversations and performances.
The teacher listens to pairs and notes speaking and listening evidence.
Pupils rate themselves on the What I can do sheet.
Reading aloud and transcription checks, three times across the two years.
Instant checks every lesson to adapt teaching straight away.

y3: ou (bonjour, nous, tout); silent final letters noticed
y4: en / an + silent letters (j'ai … ans, anglais)
Silent final consonants; the CaReFuL exceptions (c, r, f, l)
phonics.note: About 3 sound words and 1 to 2 traps per lesson. No 'tricky word' lists: those words are learnt by heart. The phonics apps also bring back sounds from earlier half terms so they are not forgotten.

grammar.y3: Chunks (HT1 to 2) → un / une with je suis (HT3) → the colour after the noun (HT3 to 4) → je vois / tu vois (HT4) → opinions joined with et / mais (HT5). No adjective agreement.
grammar.y4: Je peux / tu peux + infinitive and ne … pas (HT2) → j'ai + noun, with qui s'appelle and je n'ai pas de as chunks (HT3) → partitive and past tense heard, not produced (HT4) → polite vous (HT5) → il / elle understood (HT6).

page.audience: Partner → small group → whole class → parents or assembly (Le Zoo Rigolo !) → older pupils (Le Café Français) → a new teacher (Tout sur moi, handed on at the end of Year 4).
page.books: Two picture books anchor the two years, both in Spring 2 (HT4): Ours brun, ours brun, que vois-tu ? in Year 3 (short and repetitive) and La Chenille qui fait des trous in Year 4 (a step up, with the past tense heard). The same slot also holds a phonics checkpoint.

inclusion: The fixed core only, more scaffolding held for longer, more repetition and spaced retrieval, fewer choices at once. Use the Adapted sheets.

No single template: resources follow the child's interests and needs, with manipulatives and picture support. Pupils may step back from fast spontaneous games such as Guess Who. Use the Inclusion sheets and simple word mats.
An extension vocabulary bank and a ★ Challenge in each lesson.

These pupils usually speak and understand French well, so their focus is on reading and writing. Where it suits the pupil, they are also offered a second language, currently Spanish, to push their curiosity.
assessment: Judged at SOLO 3 (multistructural), 4 (relational) or 5 (extended abstract); below 3 is recorded as 'not yet' with a note.
Each National Curriculum code is logged twice a year (R3 once): about 4 judgements per half term, 23 per pupil per year.
For each code, report the number of pupils below SOLO 4, at SOLO 4 and at SOLO 5.
Quick checks (circulating, mini-whiteboards, thumbs) are not recorded; they shape the lesson there and then.
impact: Does each pupil's level rise between the two logged moments for the same code?
The same reading-aloud and transcription check three times across two years: a fair before/after comparison.
Dated work in books: Mon bilan, the Ours brun book, birthday cards, the Tout sur moi profile.
Self-assessment faces and the words pupils choose for 'mes mots'.
Tout sur moi goes to the next teacher: real evidence of what each pupil can do at the end of Year 4.
Keep exemplar work each term and re-check a sample of SOLO judgements against it.

think: Why does every lesson start with phonics?
It is a warm-up that prepares pupils for the lesson ahead. Through continuous practice they can decode more and more words, they grow in confidence, and their pronunciation improves.
Why is retrieval always at the beginning?
To make connections with prior learning before anything new is introduced.
Why does every lesson follow the same shape?
Routines help children feel safe and stop them feeling overwhelmed. Because the routine takes care of itself, children can concentrate on the new content.
Why do pupils see the picture before the word?
To avoid misconceptions and the bad habits that come from reading a word incorrectly. We also avoid learning French word, then English word, then image. We go from the French word to the image.
Why is grammar explained?
So children understand what they are doing, rather than only copying a pattern.
Why colour coding?
It helps children understand how a sentence works, and remember it.
Why write first and draw afterwards?
Pupils do the hard work first and then draw, so that more of their time is spent thinking about the new content.
What makes a good game?

Children use the language they know and meet no barriers, because the game is easy to follow. Games are normally played in pairs or teams, while the teacher walks around, observes and gives feedback. We avoid games where children get out of control or need to shout.
Why does the audience grow?
There is a progression from small and comfortable to wider and more challenging. Pupils get motivated and see a purpose for what they are preparing, so the learning is meaningful.
Why are there different levels of work?

We think of all our pupils. Most work at Class level. Adapted is the same work with scaffolding. A Challenge is always offered, as there are no limits. Inclusion is for those who cannot access what the rest of the class is doing, and they still feel part of the group because their work links to each day's objective.
Why so much cut and stick and joining in the Inclusion work?

The Inclusion work is designed for pupils with special educational needs (SEN). These pupils find the work accessible and more fun, so they engage. We can talk as they work, and they can discuss their learning with support staff. The same work as the rest of the class may be overwhelming, and they may not engage.
Why SOLO?
SOLO shows how deep a pupil's understanding is, not just how many answers are right. It moves from knowing separate words, to linking them into sentences, to using language in new ways.
Why Mon bilan?
It is structured and can be done under controlled conditions, so it gives clear written evidence. Speaking and listening are observed during planned activities.

grow.L1: From short questions answered with short phrases, to longer sentences with et, mais and qui s'appelle, answered in full sentences.
grow.L2: From reading new words with ou, oi and ch, to reading and spelling unseen words using every sound learnt, with free transcription.
grow.S1: From a short exchange about name, age and feelings, to longer linked conversations with extra detail and their own forms (anglais / anglaise).
grow.S2: From single descriptive sentences, to longer sentences joined with et / mais and full sentences with polite forms (s'il vous plaît).
grow.S3: From reading a page aloud with ou, oi and ch, to speaking fluently with en/an, silent letters and liaison.
grow.S4: From reading to the class, to performing for parents, then serving visiting Year 7s and presenting without reading every word.
grow.R1: From matching words and short sentences, to reading a profile in the third person and answering questions about it.
grow.R2: From picking out words in a song or patterned book, to retelling a story that includes the past tense.
grow.R3: From using the word list to find new words with support, to using the word mat independently every lesson, including extension verbs.
grow.W1: From one learnt sentence with a correctly spelt word, to adapting sentences about themselves (can / can't, a café order).
grow.W2: From describing animals with correct word order, to a full profile joined with connectives.
grow.G1: From adjective position and un / une, to ne … pas around peux, the infinitive, and choosing tu or vous with a reason.

marie: Two real toys with their own personalities. Marie, a teddy, is shy, timid, calm and quiet. Her best friend Pierre, a toy duck, is loud, cheeky and outgoing.
They began as a class mascot. It went so well that they were given personalities. Children ask about them when the teacher arrives, or if they have not been brought out.

When Marie is held up, the class sings quietly. When Pierre is held up, they sing loudly. Everyone joins in, even children who show challenging behaviour. It also helps to keep the class quiet at the end of a song, ready to listen.
So children have to use their knowledge of French to speak to them. Pupils talk to them and ask them questions.
A child who is upset or feeling down can keep Marie or Pierre at their table.
Pierre hides for this hide-and-seek game, and the class says the word louder as the seeker gets closer. Children love it.
levels: Most pupils work at this level.
Always offered, as there are no limits.
For those who cannot access what the rest of the class is doing. They still feel part of the group because their work links to each day's objective.
progressShows: Every half term adds new vocabulary and a new grammar step, so the same code is assessed on harder French: chunks, un / une and colours in Year 3; je peux + infinitive, ne … pas, j'ai and vous in Year 4.
More at the same SOLO level
Each code has its own SOLO descriptors for each unit. SOLO 4 in Year 4 asks for longer, linked sentences and more independence than SOLO 4 in Year 3 (see the table below).
Scaffolds are reduced over time. In phonics, transcription moves from a choice of 2 in Year 3 to free transcription in Year 4.
Pupils speak and write for a partner, then a group, the class, parents, older pupils and finally a new teacher.
Each code is logged twice a year, so a pupil's SOLO level for the same code can be compared across both years.
handbook.shortAnswer: The code stays the same, but the French gets harder and the SOLO level asks for more. A Year 4 pupil at SOLO 4 in S1 is doing much more than a Year 3 pupil at SOLO 4 in S1.
handbook.believe: Children learn a language when they are engaged and see a purpose for it. They use it in real scenarios and it covers their interests. Playing games allows repetition and engagement. We want them to be as involved as possible, using all they have learnt as they keep learning.
handbook.goodGame: Children use the language they know and meet no barriers, because it is easy to follow. Pairs or teams, with the teacher walking around, observing and giving feedback. We avoid games where children get out of control or need to shout.
